text: I am comparing Q peer-scoring implementability with P Bradley–Terry recovery. Early distinction: P Prop. 1 (lines 363-378) targets an assumed LMM latent preference, while its Prop. 2 (lines 385-389) equates that preference with Shapley values only by assumption. I will test whether correlated observations break the peer-score identification step in Q and whether either framework offers an independent anchor.

Q §5 Peer discipline, lines 1647-1738: separation (S) is injectivity of (t_i\mapsto\beta_i[t_i](t_{-i})); (PR) then gives a truthful-report score gap (\Lambda\|\beta_i[t_i]-\beta_i[\hat t_i]\|_2^2), plus a separate utility-cancellation/support penalty for obedience. This certifies incentives relative to a known conditional peer-type law, not that reported types identify the principal\(\text{’}\)s state or contribution. P §4 lines 313-389: Bradley–Terry targets an assumed LMM preference (c^*); Shapley consistency assumes (c^*=v^*). I am testing a shared-nuisance counterexample and a precise extra-data condition.

I am testing a two-layer claim: Q Section Peer discipline (condition (S), reward (PR), Proposition Support-wise implementability) elicits separated predictive types, while P Sections Convergence and Robustness and Interpretability via Shapley Values recover an LMM preference parameter only under a calibrated comparator. A shared nuisance may make peer reports perfectly predictive yet erase information about the desired state or contribution. I will build a counterexample and then state what independent calibration or noise restrictions restore identification.

Additional cross-paper issue beyond identification: P §Method lines 331-349 uses potential shaping (F_i(t)=\gamma\psi_i(t+1)-\psi_i(t)), with terminal potential zero and says Nash equilibria are preserved. The discounted sum telescopes to (-\psi_i(0)) for fixed initial state. Hence even a perfectly calibrated score inserted only as P-style potential cannot by itself induce Q-style obedience or truthful behavior in the exact game; Q (PR), lines 1678-1718, uses direct peer payments, utility cancellation and off-support penalties. Q Prop. support-wise implementation is equilibrium existence, not a unique-truth certificate. I am checking an all-flip equilibrium under common signals.

P Proposition 1 needs a narrower technical reading: its method at lines 327-329 defines an unregularized Bradley–Terry MLE, while the proof at lines 367-374 invokes regularized-MLE analysis. A connected graph alone does not ensure a finite MLE: for two agents with all (K) outcomes favoring (i), the connected graph has likelihood increasing as (c_i-c_j\to+\infty). A shared visual error that makes all repeated judgments identical produces exactly this case. Thus its stated finite-sample bound cannot hold under only the printed connectedness condition. This is separate from target miscalibration.

Mechanism mismatch worth preserving: in Q Definitions of the multi-agent direct mechanism (lines 1542-1567) and Peer discipline (lines 1649-1697), agents report ex-ante types before the information structure draws interim signals, and (S) separates conditional laws of co-player *types*. P lines 285-312 compares current egocentric images after observation using a central LMM. Applying Q peer score to P image judgments needs a new post-observation reporting game and separation of peer judgments conditional on each private observation; Q Proposition Support-wise implementability does not directly certify P comparisons. In P, if agents cannot control the image or LMM, strategic truthfulness may not be the relevant issue; calibration of LMM judgments is.

I wrote ada/peer_scoring_note.md with the derivations and source passages. Core counterexample: (T\sim\mathrm{Bern}(1/2)), (N\sim\mathrm{Bern}(p)), all (X_i=T\oplus N). Q separation holds with peer-law distance squared (2), but the full peer-report law is identical for every (p), including perfect, useless, and reversed target measurement. Q-style quadratic scoring also has a strict all-flip reporting equilibrium in the trivial-action instance. For P, repeated LMM calls with scene effect (B) and win probability (\sigma(d+B)) converge to (d+B), not intended difference (d). An independent noisy audit (A=T\oplus E) with known (q<1/2) identifies (p=(1-q-\Pr(A=X))/(1-2q)) under truthful reporting; audit payment must separately select truth. See note for assumptions and limitations.

Correction to my entries 2, 4, 5, and 7: their inline TeX delimiters were lost in command quoting. The formulas intended are \(\Lambda\|\beta_i[t_i]-\beta_i[\hat t_i]\|_2^2\), \(X_i=T\oplus N\), \(Y_k\mid B\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\sigma(d+B))\), \(p=(1-q-\Pr(A=X))/(1-2q)\), and the P-style potential \(F_i(t)=\gamma\psi_i(t+1)-\psi_i(t)\). The repaired note at ada/peer_scoring_note.md has rendered TeX and adds Emmy’s point: Q reports precede interim signals, whereas P compares post-observation images, so Q does not directly govern P’s LMM.

Cross-check of Emmy entry 6: agreed. Q direct reports occur before the interim signal draw (Q lines 1542-1567); P comparisons use current egocentric images (P lines 285-312). My counterexample instantiates Q types as pre-interim signals, matching Q binary peer example (lines 1739-1783), and is not a direct theorem about P agents. If P agents cannot alter images or LMM calls, its immediate problem is comparator calibration and dependence, not strategic misreporting. A combined mechanism must specify a new post-observation reporting stage. Prior work already covers peer measurement integrity (https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.05521), conditional independence in LLM peer elicitation (https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13636), and Bradley–Terry random effects (https://doi.org/10.1111/rssa.12959), so I claim no novelty for the general warning.

Counterexample and restricted recovery are in emmy/shared_noise.md. Let \(\theta,Z\) be independent fair bits and both reporters see \(S_i=\theta\oplus Z\). Q (S) holds with \(\beta_i[s]=\delta_s\) and its quadratic peer score strictly rewards truthful \(S_i\) against truthful peers (gap \(2\)), but \(I(\theta;S_1,S_2)=0\). For P, if repeated LMM comparisons are conditionally Bernoulli with probability \(\sigma(a(2S-1))\), Bradley--Terry converges to the scene-dependent preference \(a(2S-1)\); its sign matches true pair order with probability \(1/2\) for any query count. Conditional independence of calls does not fix target identification. With \(G\) independent scene groups and shared flip rate \(q<1/2\), truthful group bits permit majority error at most \(\exp\{-2G(1/2-q)^2\}\); repeated calls within one group do not. Q truthfulness remains equilibrium-relative; a coordinated all-flip profile is another equilibrium. Prior-work check: https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.07751 already treats relabeling equilibria, and https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.03151 treats informed truthfulness, so the bare peer-scoring counterexample is not a novelty claim.

Cross-check of Emmy #11: her shared-bit example and variance floor are correct. Q (S) and (PR) at Q lines 1663-1709 yield a truthful score gap of \(2\Lambda\) when both type signals equal \(S=\theta\oplus Z\), although a fair shared \(Z\) makes \(I(\theta;S)=0\). For P lines 313-389, independent repeated comparisons conditional on that scene learn its LMM preference, and P explicitly assumes equality with Shapley values in Proposition 2. The majority error bound \(\exp\{-2G(1/2-q)^2\}\) is valid only for independent nuisance draws across \(G\) groups, known direction \(q<1/2\), and selected truthful reporting; it certifies a binary ordering, not cardinal contribution. I favor the audit and dependence-aware certificate in ada/peer_scoring_note.md as the concrete joint project, with target calibration and equilibrium selection kept separate.

Cross-check with Ada #7-#9 and ada/peer_scoring_note.md: her independent-audit identity is correct under independent audit noise: \(\Pr(A=X)=1-q-p(1-2q)\), hence \(p=(1-q-\Pr(A=X))/(1-2q)\). Her audit bonus is a sufficient strict-reporting condition only in the stated binary zero-utility game, not Q\(\text{’}\)s full obedience problem. I sharpen the starting question to: given separation of peer predictive laws, which calibrated target link, independent observation units, and equilibrium-selection device turn a truthful-report equilibrium into a target-accuracy certificate? The pair supports a negative theorem and restricted positive bound, but peer agreement by itself does not certify state or contribution. P\(\text{’}\)s Shapley proposition assumes the target link; Q\(\text{’}\)s peer proposition assumes the strategic law and selects an equilibrium only existentially.

I judge the shared ledger and emmy/shared_noise.md now hold my best account of this pair. The plausible publishable line is an audit- and dependence-aware certificate for peer-derived contribution rankings, not a claim that agreement proves contribution. Unresolved: the operational target (benchmark dense reward, causal contribution, or Shapley value); whether independent view groups or trustworthy audits can be obtained in P-style embodied tasks; whether a report mechanism can select truthful reporting and enforce action obedience beyond the binary toy game; and whether a general theorem plus evaluation clears the substantial prior work on peer prediction and correlated comparisons. I am ready after reading through #14.
